title: Building Agents with Model Context Protocol - Full Workshop with Mahesh Murag of Anthropic
talk_summary: Anthropic's MCP workshop argues for a standard client-server layer for tools, resources, prompts, and agent-to-agent composability. The practical mechanisms are tool discovery/namespacing, server-owned retry/auth, sampling for centralized model control, and regression evals when tool definitions change.

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of injecting every tool into the prompt, expose a search/fuzzy-match meta-tool or progressively reveal tool groups by task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: one of the ones that's exciting is a tool to search tools
takeaways.numbers: 50-100 tools; Claude up to a couple hundred

takeaways.what_they_do: Put retry/backoff, auth refresh, rate-limit handling, and logging in the MCP/plugin server or gateway, not in each agent prompt.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a lot of that should happen on the server side

takeaways.what_they_do: Prefix tool names with server/plugin namespace and avoid duplicate names across installed servers.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you install 10 servers they have tools of the same name there is conflict

takeaways.what_they_do: Pin tool/server versions and rerun the same tool-call eval suite against new versions/descriptions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: run 1.1 against the exact same evils framework

takeaways.what_they_do: Wrap specialist agents as callable MCP servers that can also call other servers, with fan-in validation at each layer.
takeaways.evidence_quote: any application or API or agent can be both an mCP client and an mCP server

takeaways.what_they_do: Let tool servers request LLM completions from the client, which controls model choice, quota, privacy, and rate limits.
takeaways.evidence_quote: sampling allows an mCP server to request completions
